segments.title: HMS Rutherford's American-built origin
segments.body: HMS Rutherford, K558, was an American-built escort that served in the Royal Navy as a Captain-class frigate. She was originally constructed in the United States as a Buckley-class destroyer escort, so the American and British classifications refer to the same ship. Her Royal Navy service lasted from 1943 to 1945, in the final years of the Second World War. Her work as a coastal-forces command frigate formed part of the Royal Navy's response to E-boats.

evidence.note: The introduction links Rutherford to the Royal Navy's response to E-boats, identifies K558 as a Captain-class frigate built as a Buckley-class destroyer escort, and gives her Royal Navy service dates.
The explanation of information sharing with motor torpedo boats identifies Rutherford's coastal-forces command role.

segments.summary: HMS Rutherford was a Captain-class frigate built in the United States as a Buckley-class destroyer escort and employed by the Royal Navy from 1943 to 1945.

segments.title: HMS Rutherford's speed and escort endurance
segments.body: Rutherford displaced roughly 1,400 tons and measured about 93 metres long and 11 metres across, with a draught of roughly 2.5 to 2.7 metres. Her machinery used two Foster Wheeler express D-type water-tube boilers and developed about 13,500 shaft horsepower, enough for a top speed of roughly 24 knots. That speed was sufficient for her role even though she was not especially fast. Her range was about 5,500 nautical miles at 15 knots.

evidence.note: Rutherford displaced roughly 1,400 tons, measured about 93 by 11 metres, used two Foster Wheeler boilers, made about 24 knots, and ranged 5,500 nautical miles at 15 knots.

segments.summary: Rutherford combined a top speed of roughly 24 knots with a range of 5,500 nautical miles at 15 knots.

segments.title: HMS Rutherford's guns and anti-submarine armament
segments.body: Rutherford carried three 3-inch guns, approximately 76 mm in calibre, and one twin 40 mm Bofors mounting. Her 20 mm Oerlikon battery ranged from seven to sixteen guns at different points in her career, with the number increasing as D-Day approached. A Mark 10 Hedgehog anti-submarine mortar and depth charges gave her weapons for attacking submerged targets. This armament combined close-range gun defence with dedicated anti-submarine weapons on a coastal-forces command frigate.

evidence.note: Rutherford carried three 3-inch guns of roughly 76 mm calibre, a twin 40 mm mounting, an enlarged 20 mm battery near D-Day, Hedgehog, and depth charges.

segments.summary: Rutherford carried three 3-inch guns, a twin 40 mm Bofors mounting, up to sixteen 20 mm Oerlikons, Hedgehog, and depth charges.

segments.title: A radar-equipped command ship for motor torpedo boats
segments.body: Rutherford's sensor fit comprised SA and SL radar sets, Type 144 ASDIC, a medium-frequency (MF) direction-finding antenna, and a Type FH4 high-frequency (HF) direction-finding antenna. A coastal-forces command ship gathered information and passed it to the smaller motor torpedo boats, providing an information and coordination centre for the flotilla. The Royal Navy developed these frigates for that role and used the ships it had available. Destroyers sometimes took over because they often carried the same equipment and more, allowing a destroyer flotilla leader to fill the command role on particular operations. For this command work, sensors and information flow mattered more than armament.

evidence.note: Rutherford's sensors included the Type FH4 high-frequency direction-finding antenna at 1:55-1:57, supporting an information-sharing role that the Royal Navy assigned to available command frigates or, occasionally, destroyer flotilla leaders.

segments.summary: SA and SL radar, Type 144 ASDIC, and medium- and high-frequency direction-finding equipment supported Rutherford's role as a coastal-forces command frigate.
